title: Scientists Say a 'Godzilla' El Niño Is Building in the Pacific. India May Be Its Biggest Casualty.
excerpt: Three-quarters of climate models now predict the developing El Niño could reach 2.5°C of warming — rivalling the strongest event ever recorded. For India, the stakes are existential: a weakened monsoon, surging food prices, and a power grid already running at record demand.
body:
An enormous pool of abnormally warm water is massing beneath the surface of the equatorial Pacific, and three-quarters of the world's leading climate models now agree on what it means: the El Niño event building for later this year could rival the most powerful ever recorded.

The European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service reported this week that 75 per cent of forecast models predict the developing El Niño will reach 2.5°C of warming in the Niño 3.4 region — a threshold that would place it alongside the catastrophic 1997–98 event, the strongest in the modern instrumental record. The World Meteorological Organization now puts the probability of El Niño conditions between June and August at 80 per cent, rising to 90 per cent through November.

Climate scientists interviewed by AFP said 2027 would likely surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record.

For India, the implications are not abstract. They are agricultural, economic, and political.

## The Monsoon Is Already Struggling

The southwest monsoon, which irrigates nearly half of India's farmland and determines the fate of a rural economy that still employs close to half the workforce, arrived three days late this year on 4 June. As of the second week of June, rainfall is running 18 per cent below the long-period average.

The India Meteorological Department has already lowered its seasonal forecast to 90 per cent of normal — the threshold below which a monsoon is classified as deficient. El Niño years historically weaken the monsoon by disrupting the atmospheric circulation patterns that pull moisture from the Indian Ocean across the subcontinent.

There is one countervailing force. Australia's Bureau of Meteorology reported that the Indian Ocean Dipole, a separate climate oscillation, could turn positive during August and September. A positive IOD can boost monsoon rainfall even in El Niño years, and the interplay between the two systems will likely determine whether India gets a merely weak monsoon or a disastrous one.

But the balance of risk is tilting the wrong way. Sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region crossed the El Niño threshold of +0.80°C as of 7 June, reaching +0.81°C. All models indicate continued warming through the northern hemisphere summer.

## Food Prices, Power Demand, and Water

The cascade effects of a strong El Niño on India are well-documented and mutually reinforcing.

A weakened monsoon reduces yields of rice, pulses, cotton, soybean, and maize. India is already contending with food inflation driven by the Iran war's impact on fertiliser supply chains and global energy costs. A simultaneous crop shortfall would push prices higher at precisely the moment when households can least absorb it.

Hotter-than-normal temperatures — a hallmark of El Niño years — drive up electricity consumption. India recorded an all-time peak power demand of approximately 265 gigawatts recently, and sustained heat with patchy rainfall would strain grids further, particularly in states that depend on hydropower.

Reduced rainfall also means lower reservoir levels. Cities that are already rationing water would face deeper shortages, and hydropower generation in rain-dependent regions like the northeast and the Western Ghats would decline.

## The Economic Compound

The timing could hardly be worse. India's economy is already absorbing the shock of the Iran war. Oil prices above $95 per barrel have pushed the current account deficit wider, driven the rupee to record lows near 97 per dollar, and forced the Reserve Bank of India into a defensive posture.

The RBI cut its fiscal 2027 growth forecast to a range of 6.6 to 6.9 per cent. Inflation crossed the central bank's 4 per cent target in May for the first time in 15 months. The combination of an energy price shock and a potential agricultural supply shock is the scenario that keeps Indian policymakers awake at night.

"India is set for a series of supply shocks," Michael Langham, emerging markets economist at Aberdeen Investments, said. "The ability of the RBI to look through the energy price shock from the Strait of Hormuz will be increasingly difficult given the overlapping nature of these supply shocks."

The government has already begun contingency planning. It has mapped 197 districts across the country that are most vulnerable to monsoon failure and drawn up crop-specific response plans. But preparedness and prevention are different things, and no amount of planning can conjure rain.

## What to Watch

El Niño typically peaks between November and January, but the ocean–atmosphere coupling that amplifies it accelerates during the summer months. The next eight to twelve weeks will reveal whether this event stays moderate or becomes the monster that climate watchers are increasingly calling a "Godzilla" El Niño.

Scientists stress that stronger events raise the odds of more severe impacts but do not guarantee them. Long-range forecasts carry significant uncertainty. And the Indian Ocean Dipole remains a wild card that could partially offset El Niño's impact on the monsoon.

But the base case has shifted. What was a modest probability six months ago is now the central forecast of the world's most sophisticated climate models. India, already reeling from the Iran war's economic fallout, may be about to discover what happens when two simultaneous supply shocks hit an economy of 1.4 billion people at once.
